title: Nero blames the Christians
saying: quōs per flāgitia invīsōs vulgus Chrīstiānōs appellābat
author: Tacitus
setting: Rome after the fire of AD 64

edition.section: Annals 15.44, from "sed non ope humana" to "celebranturque" (sections 2–3 in the usual numbering)

source_text: sed non ope humana, non largitionibus principis aut deum placamentis decedebat infamia quin iussum incendium crederetur. ergo abolendo rumori Nero subdidit reos et quaesitissimis poenis adfecit quos per flagitia invisos vulgus Christianos appellabat. auctor nominis eius Christus Tiberio imperitante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio adfectus erat; repressaque in praesens exitiabilis superstitio rursum erumpebat, non modo per Iudaeam, originem eius mali, sed per urbem etiam quo cuncta undique atrocia aut pudenda confluunt celebranturque.
excerpt_note: Three sentences from the middle of chapter 15.44. Fisher's text, as encoded, has chapter but no section numbers; "15.44.2–3" follows the usual modern division and was not checked against a numbered edition. Sentences begin in lower case as in the file. Fisher prints Christianos; the oldest manuscript seems to have had Chrestianos (see the essay).

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: Chrīstus, Chrīstiānōs: long ī, following the Dickinson College Commentaries' macronized Pliny; the Greek Christos has a long iota. Not machine-checked.
flāgitia: long ā, the usual dictionary quantity; not machine-checked.
plācāmentīs, largītiōnibus, dēcēdēbat, īnfāmia, rūmōrī, quaesītissimīs, prōcūrātōrem, Pīlātum, exitiābilis, Iūdaeam, atrōcia, cōnfluunt: standard dictionary quantities; not machine-checked.
cūncta: long ū before nct, following the app lexicon (DCC cūnctus).
adfēcit, adfectus: the edition's spelling of afficiō (ad- not assimilated); the macron in adfēcit follows fēcī.

translation: Yet neither human efforts nor the emperor's gifts nor offerings to placate the gods could rid him of the scandal: people went on believing that the fire had been set on orders. So, to kill the rumour, Nero put forward culprits and inflicted the most elaborate punishments on people hated for their outrages, whom the common people called Christians. The founder of the name, Christus, had been executed in the reign of Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate; the deadly superstition, suppressed for a while, was breaking out again, not only in Judaea, where the evil began, but even in the City, where everything horrible or shameful flows in from every side and finds a following.
translation_note: Quīn after a negative ("nothing removed the scandal") introduces what the scandal was: "that the fire was believed to have been ordered". Deum is the short genitive plural of deus (= deōrum). The sentence about Christus is in the pluperfect (adfectus erat): it explains the name, as background. Celebrantur here means "are thronged, made popular", not "celebrated" in a religious sense.

essay.t: In AD 64 a great fire swept through Rome.
Tacitus notes that some people recorded its start as 19 July, the day on which the Senones had once burned the captured city.
In this passage he says that neither human effort, nor the emperor's handouts, nor rites to appease the gods removed the belief that the fire had been ordered, so Nero produced culprits.
Suetonius states outright that Nero set the fire, and lists the punishment of Christians, "a kind of men of a new and harmful superstition", among Nero's measures without linking it to the fire.
Tacitus was born around AD 56, so he was a boy at the time; he later governed the province of Asia, probably in 112–113.
He names no sources; Lawrence Mykytiuk suggests he may have learned about Christians as governor of Asia, where he probably supervised trials of accused Christians.
In my reading, it is evidence for an upper-class Roman view of Christians, and for what Rome knew of Christus's execution.
It calls Pilate procurator, but the inscription found at Caesarea in 1961 calls him prefect, as usually restored: [PRAEF]ECTUS IUDA[EA]E.
Mykytiuk argues the passage is authentic, partly from its "true Tacitean" Latin; the classicist Peter Gainsford agrees, though he doubts it is independent evidence for the historical Jesus.
Richard Carrier argues the opposite: that the sentence about Christus is a Christian interpolation of the fourth century or later.
I call authenticity the majority view on the strength of these sources, not a survey of the scholarship.

Fisher prints Christianos, but Gainsford argues from the oldest manuscript of this book (Florence, Laurentian Library, Plut. 68.2) that the scribe first wrote Chrestianos and someone scraped the e into an i, while Christus in the next line is original.
If so, Tacitus may have reported the crowd's form of the name, "Chrestians", beside the founder's correct name.
How far per flagitia invisos is Tacitus's own judgement is debated; he later calls the victims guilty, yet says they were convicted less of arson than of hatred of the human race.

questions.q: What title does Tacitus give Pontius Pilate, and what does the inscription from Caesarea show?
options: Procurator; the inscription calls him prefect
Prefect; the inscription calls him procurator
Consul; the inscription calls him a king
Legate; the inscription calls him tribune

questions.q: In the oldest manuscript of this book, what seems to have happened to the word for "Christians"?
options: An original e was scraped into an i
The word was squeezed into the margin
Christus was altered to read Chrestus
The whole sentence was added later

questions.q: How does Suetonius's account of the fire differ from Tacitus's?
options: Suetonius says plainly that Nero set it
Suetonius blames the Christians for it
Suetonius calls it a pure accident
